chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
The mortgage is the largest debt of most households. Understanding fixed vs variable rate, term and amortization helps you choose a loan suited to your risk tolerance and your situation.

This guide clarifies these concepts and the questions to ask before signing.

2026 edition note: rates change constantly; confirm with a mortgage broker. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

The mortgage is the largest debt of most households. This guide clarifies the fixed vs variable trade-off, the difference between term and amortization, the clauses that matter, and how to adapt the loan to your life.

Note (2026 edition): rates change constantly; always confirm with a mortgage broker.

chapters.title: Fixed rate vs variable rate
chapters.html:
Understanding the main trade-off.

It's every borrower's big choice, and it comes down to your risk tolerance:

  • Fixed rate: the same for the whole term. Predictable payments, peace of mind, but often a slightly higher starting rate.
  • Variable rate: follows market fluctuations. Can cost less if rates drop or stay low, but exposes you to payment or interest increases.

In short: fixed buys predictability, variable bets on the market. Neither is “better” in absolute terms.

Ask yourself a simple question: would a payment increase keep you up at night? Fixed buys predictability (at the cost of an often slightly higher starting rate); variable bets on the market (possible savings, but the risk of an increase). Neither is “better” in absolute terms.

Emilie's tip

Ask yourself a simple question: would a payment increase of $150 to $300 a month keep you up at night? If so, fixed is often worth its small extra cost for the peace of mind.

chapters.title: The term and the amortization
chapters.html:
Telling apart two often-confused concepts.

These two words look alike but mean very different things:

  • Amortization: the total time to repay the loan (often 25 years).
  • Term: the length of the current contract (often 5 years), at the end of which you renew under new conditions.

A longer amortization reduces the monthly payment, but increases the total interest paid. At each end of term, you renegotiate: it's a key moment to adjust your strategy.

Don't confuse amortization (the total repayment period, often 25 years) and term (the length of the current contract, often 5 years). At each end of term, you renegotiate: it's a key moment to shop around. Don't just accept your renewal — make lenders compete two to three months before the deadline.

Emilie's tip

Don't just accept your term renewal. Two or three months before the deadline, shop around and make lenders compete: that's often where you save the most, without changing houses.

chapters.title: The clauses that matter
chapters.html:
Looking beyond the rate.

The advertised rate is only the visible part. These clauses can cost — or save — you a lot:

  • Prepayment penalties: sometimes very high if your life changes (a move, a separation).
  • Accelerated repayment: extra payments allowed, to pay off faster.
  • Portability: transferring the loan to another property.
  • Open vs closed loan: flexibility versus rate.

The lowest rate isn't always the best loan: a rigid clause can cost a lot at the wrong moment.

The advertised rate is only the visible part: prepayment penalties (sometimes very high if your life changes), accelerated repayments, portability, open vs closed loan. Before signing for an “unbeatable” rate, ask how the penalty is calculated.

Emilie's tip

Before signing for an “unbeatable” rate, ask how the prepayment penalty is calculated. At some lenders, it can amount to several thousand dollars.

chapters.title: Getting the right support to finance
chapters.objective: Choosing the right person to deal with.
chapters.html:
Choosing the right person to deal with.

You don't have to shop alone. Two main paths:

  • Your financial institution: simple if you're already a client there, but a single product line.
  • The mortgage broker: compares several lenders for you, often at no cost to the borrower.

In both cases, compare the rate and the conditions. A pre-approval gives you a confirmed amount and a guaranteed rate to shop with peace of mind.

Two paths to finance: your institution (simple if you're a client, but a single line) or a mortgage broker (compares several lenders, often at no cost to you). In both cases, compare the rate AND the conditions, and get a pre-approval to shop with peace of mind.

Emilie's tip

A good mortgage broker usually costs you nothing and can find conditions your bank won't offer you spontaneously. It's worth at least a conversation.

chapters.title: Adapting your loan to your life
chapters.objective: Choosing according to your real situation.
chapters.html:
Choosing according to your real situation.

The “right” loan depends less on the economic headlines than on your reality:

  • Job and income stability: the more solid it is, the more variable is conceivable.
  • Horizon: do you plan to keep the property a long time?
  • Financial cushion: could you absorb a payment increase?
  • Plans: a growing family, a career change, a probable resale.

A choice aligned with your life is worth more than a perfect rate on paper but uncomfortable day to day.

The “right” loan depends less on the headlines than on YOUR reality: job stability, holding horizon, financial cushion, life plans. There's no shame in choosing fixed even when “everyone” praises variable: the best loan is the one that lets you sleep soundly.

Emilie's tip

There's no shame in choosing fixed even when “everyone” says variable wins. The best loan is the one that lets you sleep soundly.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Assess my risk tolerance (fixed vs variable).
  2. Meet a mortgage broker.

Within 30 days

  1. Compare the rate AND the conditions (penalties, portability).
  2. Choose a suitable amortization and term.

Next

  1. Re-shop at each term renewal.

To choose well

  1. Assess my risk tolerance and meet a mortgage broker.
  2. Compare the rate AND the conditions (penalties, portability) and re-shop at each renewal.
